projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with T. L. Conner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: This is an interview with -- is it G.L.?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: T.L.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: T.L. Connor from Albertsville, Alabama, and conducted on the 6th of July, 2001. And Mr. Connor was a member of the battleship U.S.S. South Dakota, and I'm the interviewer, Arthur R. Huseboe, and we conducted this interview at the Ramkota Hotel in Sioux Falls, South Dakota during the reunion of the crew of the battleship. And then will you just speak your name and your address so that we can get the sound. Mike, you go ahead.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: T.L. Connor, [address deleted]. Telephone number [number deleted].

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay. Good. Now we'll -- how about your enlistment? How was it that you enlisted in the Navy?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: How what?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How -- how did it come about?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I -- I just wanted to get away from home and join the Navy. I didn't want to join the Army.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay. And how old were you? You told me earlier.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: 18 years old.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: 18 years old. And you dropped out of high school, didn't you, to join?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Right. Right. I joined May the 8th, 1940.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: May the 8th 19-- oh, you did, 1940. Before the war had broken out?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay. And you chose the Navy just because?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I didn't want to walk.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You didn't want to walk. Well, that will do it. Okay. And then where did go for your training for naval seaman?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I enlisted in Nashville, Tennessee, sworn in --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- and I went to Norfolk, Virginia.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- for eight weeks' training.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Then I was assigned to a U.S.S. Prairie AD-15, which is a destroyer tender. I put it in commission in Philadelphia.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: In 19-- well, it would be mid-1940.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we operated in and out from Philadelphia to Guantanamo Bay in Newport News -- I mean Newport, Rhode Island, and up to Argentia, Newfoundland for about 18 months.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And then I was transferred from there back to Philadelphia to put the South Dakota in commission.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Okay. So you -- you were assigned to the U.S. South Dakota when? How did you get assigned there, to the South Dakota?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: In March of --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: March of '42, I guess.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: March of '42. And what was your rating, your specialty?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I was seaman first class when I was on the South Dakota.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay. And what were some of your duties?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: We -- our cleaning station was the superstructure on the South Dakota from -- from about the main deck all the way up to the yard arms.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And it was our duty to keep it clean and have to paint it when it needed it.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And I painted the yard arms because the other fellows were afraid to get out on it. It was about 100 foot up, I'd guess. And I volunteered to paint the yard arms.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we -- that was our cleaning station.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup. Okay. The most hazardous action that you went through, the most dangerous, hazardous action?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Oh, we had -- in the battle of Santa Cruz, which was an air battle, all we was doing is following in the aircraft guns at the enemy.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Which we have a record of shooting down 32 planes. And the captain got wounded when a shrapnel hit the turret number -- number one, I believe, turret or number two maybe.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And a piece of shrapnel hit him. But I wasn't wounded at all.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Were you on a gun? Were you manning a --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I was on a five-inch gun, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, five-inch gun?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Do you know if you hit any Jap planes?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah, well, I -- I don't know for sure, but somebody did.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Somebody did, yeah. And anybody in your group get wounded or killed?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No, not that I know of.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, okay. And then were you also at Sabo Island?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah, Sabo Island.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: It was a night battle. The best I can remember, it started about half past 12:00.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Uh-hmm. Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: That would be 00:30 minutes.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And it was dark.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And everybody was scared.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I'm sure.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we sideswiped a coral reef, but it didn't do -- it didn't seem to do any damage.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, God.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: But the next day, we -- being the biggest majority of the wounded people or the wounded got killed was in the superstructure --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- that was our job to help tow them down.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And I noticed one room that I looked in, and it was about knee deep in water, and you could see a man's head --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- like a half a watermelon --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- floating around.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And that was -- that was really trying.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, you bet. Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And I put my hand up on the ledge to kind of brace myself, I guess, and the man fainted -- fainted, rolled off in my hand.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: So we gathered him up and had to carry him down several flights of steps.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup. Yup.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And laid him out on the fantail, which was -- everybody had a long face because the shipmates, I think 50 or 60 men got killed, and none of them was in my division. But this was -- this was one thing that kind of affected me a little.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Uh-hmm. Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we had a -- one night we was transferring ammunition to another ship and a tackle pulled loose from a turret and hit an electrician in the back of the head and killed him. And the next day we buried this man with military honors, with planes and all that. And he was -- when they slid him off the side of the ship, we could feel the water splash up on us, and that was -- that was kind of sad.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And that's -- then after this we -- this battle at Sabo Island, we went into New Caledonia.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And all the ships present knew about it, and they was lined up. They could see the ship was pretty well shot up. And they was lined up and give us the salute as we came in. And then the kind of sad part was we was -- had orders to return to the states, New York.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: New York City.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: New York City.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Well, they -- they had -- they needed some more men for duty on some of these ships, so they transferred all -- so many men from each division. And I seen boys crying because they -- they wanted to come back.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And this was kind of sad. The good thing was I wasn't one of the ones they transferred. I think really what they done, and this is true to the Navy, they transferred the goof-offs.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh. That's been done before.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: That's been done before. So I remember the way -- the trip back to the states, they -- we had a destroyer escort for awhile out to protect us from the submarine, Jap submarine, but then we went the rest of the way by ourselves, full steam, and went through the canal. And then went -- got through the canal, the destroyers picked us up to escort us to New York. Well, it was rough, the water was rough, and the captain -- of course the battleship could plow through it. And the captain was going so fast, the destroyer is telling him, "Slow down. We can't take it this fast." So, anyway, he said, "Well, you can come on. I'm going home." That's common knowledge.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we got to New York and the -- and the -- and the pride that we felt as we went in past the Statue of Liberty.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: We knew that we had just come from a couple of battles --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- to protect.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- that and we was proud.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You bet. You bet.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we still are.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You bet.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And we stayed in the Brooklyn Navy yard for about three months to get repaired.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup. Yup.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And I wasn't afraid to go on liberty and walk by myself or whoever was with me. At that time it was safe to be out.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You bet.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Then we got a 30-day leave, and that was enjoyable.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: I'm sure it was.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And then after this, we went to -- we -- I think it was called the biggest convoy ever made, we went with a convoy all the way to Russia, Murmansk, Russia. Of course we didn't go in port. We just went part way.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I think the theory was that we might draw out the -- the German battleships. And then we had some battleships where we could --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Was it the (turpets?)? The (turpets?), was that one of them?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah, they was -- yeah. they never did come out. And the best I can remember is it was always foggy and cloudy and damp, and it was -- you couldn't see the end of the ship. There's lots of them, a lot of destroyers.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Anyway, we turned back when we got safe in Murmansk, and went to Scapa Flow, Scotland. And I remember going over the Liberty in Scapa Flow and went in a barn like thing and they had beer, and the -- the British sailor wanted to buy me a beer. So we drunk a beer, and I couldn't hardly understand him and he couldn't understand me, I don't guess, too much. But, anyway, we're on our way back. After a few days, we went to Iceland and we anchored in one of those fjords in Iceland, and we had a chance to transfer one man from each deck division back to the states. And I was the only one in my division from Alabama, so they let me go. And we left the ship at 10 o'clock at night, and it was still -- the sun was still shining.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And a fellar -- one fellar offered me $200 for my orders. But I wanted to go as bad as he did and I had the opportunity. So, anyway, it took us about a month to go back to the States on an old eight-knot steamer, an old rust tub steamer. And they put us on lookout, and I remember one night I was on lookout from 12:00 to 4:00, and it was -- it was bright moonlight, and I was watching 'cause this thing didn't have no way to protect itself.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: So I had good eyes. I was about 20 years old then, 22. So I seen a ship off in the distance, and they had a voice tube, and the voice tube on a merchant ship is different than it is on a naval ship. You just talk into these. But I hollered into it. And the officer of the deck come running out and said, "You woke the captain up." And he come out with his little old nightcap hanging down, and he pulled out a telescope about this long and looked through it.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: He said, "Goddamn, boy, did you see that?" I said, "Yes." He said, "Well, I'm going to go back to bed. If you're the lookout, I ain't going to worry." So we made it safe back to New York.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Then we caught a train to Mobile, and that's about the end of my experience with South Dakota.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Boy, that's exciting.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Now, is there anything else you wanted to ask?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Well, let's see. I was going to ask a little more about -- about heroic actions by yourself or others on -- during those battles. Were there some commendations given, some recommendations given to people right after the battles?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: There may have been. I didn't -- I didn't get wounded and I didn't deserve anything, so I was just doing my job.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay. Were you seasick at all?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Never. Never seasick.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Not on the South Dakota. How about on the destroyers?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Nope. Never was seasick. But I've seen 'em yearning to die from seasickness.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Now, did you get bored?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: We was mostly occupied so much, you didn't have time to think about home or getting bored or nothing.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How about bad weather?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Bad weather is bad on destroyers. On the battleship, it's not much.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: It doesn't matter. It doesn't matter, yeah. Although I heard there was one -- Now, were you on the South Dakota when it ran into that whale?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No, I don't -- well, I must have been. I think that was on the way to Murmansk.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I don't -- I heard them talking about it, and I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You don't remember it. Well, you couldn't be everywhere, you know.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: If that wasn't your duty station --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Some things you can remember and some things you don't.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure. Sure. Sure. How about submarines, did you see any or --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: We chased submarines when I was on another ship.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Not with the South Dakota, though.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How about being being afraid of submarines, were you worried about them a lot?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah. Sure, I was.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: The most -- the most scared I was ever was on this destroyer. We was chasing this sub all day or two. We finally sunk it. But I was -- everybody wasn't on the watch at one time. So I was laying in the bed and they -- they shot a K-Gun with a depth charge and -- and as they did, the lap -- We done screw a lot, but just a little bit. But, anyway, the shock of this K-Gun going off turned this light on just momentarily, and I said "Oh, my God, they blowed the side of the ship out." Then I -- in a split second I knew what happened, see.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Sure. Sure. How about bombing attacks? You were on a gun.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Do you remember any of the things that happened relating to, oh, the Enterprise was nearby at Sabo Island -- or, I mean, at Santa Cruz?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Santa Cruz, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Santa Cruz.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Well, there was a Hornet. The Hornet got sunk.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And the well got damaged so bad that they -- the Americans sunk it.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And I could see that smoke.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You could see that.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: How about the Enterprise, could you see that at all?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No, I couldn't see -- I don't believe I noticed the Enterprise. Anyway, a destroyer got a hit on the bow.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: And the destroyer had a smart captain, I suppose, so he cut across and he hit the wave that the South Dakota was making, and the water come up on the foc'sle and put the fire out.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Put the fire out. How about torpedos during that battle, did you --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No, I don't believe there was any torpedos. I don't know --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You didn't see any, or notice them?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No, I didn't, uhn-uhn.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: This was strictly an air battle. We never did see ships.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, but I mean torpedos from the ships -- from the planes coming in.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, no, I didn't --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: We heard --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I couldn't see. I was in the upper handling room.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah. We heard that the South Dakota really maneuvered.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You got a --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You got an appointment?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You got to get to the --

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I need to go for some --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Okay. All right.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Are you about done with this?

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, I'm just about done. Is there anything you want to add to -- to the story?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I believe I told you all the important things.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: You enjoyed getting home to -- Did you go back to Alabama on your leave, that 30-day leave?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Folks -- could you talk about your experiences?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Well, not much. People didn't want to talk about it much then.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: No. Yeah, yeah. Well, it was confidential or top secret or whatever.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: No. Well, the ship was. They told us not to talk about the --

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: -- the Waterloo Old Nameless was.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh. Oh, they didn't want to -- oh, you couldn't say it was the South Dakota?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Uhn-uhn. Right, right. You wasn't supposed to. But I guess some of them did.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Some of them did.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: They kept it secret a long time.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: I know they did.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: We had a great captain.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: A great captain.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I've had some that was psychotic though. They was terrible. On other ships.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: On other ships, yeah. Well, the South Dakota had a great -- a great record, a great campaign record, just outstanding.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Yeah. I really think President Truman, I feel hard on him. The top brass in the Navy wanted to -- the Japanese signing on the South Dakota 'cause she was the queen on the fleet.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Had more battle stars than any other ship.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: But then Truman was from Missouri. He said, "We'll have it on the Missouri." If I'd have been the admirals, I'd have say we'll make out like we gonna have it, but they could have done it. There wasn't nothing he could do about it. Of course, he could have played heck with them admirals.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, I suppose. But you were right -- you were berthed right next to the Missouri, weren't you, in Tokyo Bay? Weren't you the next ship over?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: Well, no, I wasn't on that ship.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Oh, you -- that's right. That's right.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I was on the destroyer. I was -- I was in there, but I was in a different place.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Yeah, different place. Oh, yeah, that's right. Well, I really appreciate your taking the time.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: And you got to run another errand?

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I enjoyed it. You done good. I don't know how I done.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: Well, you did fine.

sp.speaker: T. L. Conner
sp.p: I better be a running.

sp.speaker: Arthur R. Huseboe
sp.p: All right.
Conclusion of interview]
